https://english.radio.cz/trauma-betrayal.text: CS DE EN ES FR РУ УК Trauma of betrayal we should learn from: Political leaders honor victims of 1968 invasion Facebook Twitter Trauma of betrayal we should learn from: Political leaders honor victims of 1968 invasion 5:49 ⨯ Trauma of betrayal we should learn from: Political leaders honor victims of 1968 invasion https://english.radio.cz/trauma-betrayal-we-should-learn-political-leaders-honor-victims-1968-invasion-8895262#player=on Copy Share on social media Facebook X August 21, 1968, went down in Czechoslovak history as the day that Soviet-led Warsaw Pact troops crushed the Prague Spring reforms and the hopes of millions of people yearning for freedom and democracy. At a solemn ceremony outside the Czech Radio building, political leaders laid wreaths to honor those who lost their lives in the invasion and highlighted the role of free media – then and now. Twenty years after the Communist Party seized power in Czechoslovakia in February 1948, the Prague Spring emerged after a dark period – a time of hope and belief in a better future that, however, lasted only a very short time. It is primarily associated with Alexander Dubček, who advocated what became known as “socialism with a human face.” The movement was brutally suppressed on August 21, when troops from the Soviet Union and other allied countries invaded Czechoslovakia, 58 years ago. The Czechoslovak Radio building on Vinohradská Street, now home to Czech Radio, was one of the invaders’ main targets. Citizens confronted the occupying troops in what became known as the “Battle for Czechoslovak Radio,” in which 17 people were killed. As every year on this day, a solemn commemorative ceremony was held at the entrance to the building on Vinohradská Street with political representatives laying wreaths in the presence of a guard of honor and to the sounds of a brass band. The ceremony was followed by a series of speeches, starting with Czech Radio Director-General René Zavoral. “Many historians believe that those few months of relative freedom known as the Prague Spring were an experience that helped us endure the following two decades of totalitarian oppression. If we refuse to forget that day of betrayal, shame and national humiliation, it is not merely out of a sense of duty to mourn our fallen and seriously wounded fellow citizens. We remember because this event remains an unhealed wound and offers many lessons that remain relevant even today.” Above the heads of those gathered outside the Czech Radio building, numerous banners could be seen expressing support for the independence of public-service media. They were a response to the months-long debate over abolishing licence fees and changing the way Czech Radio and Czech Television are funded. Many people view the government’s proposal as an attack on media freedom. The parallel between defending public radio in the past and doing so today therefore also featured in Zavoral’s speech. “The fact that the largest confrontation between the occupiers and true Czech patriots took place here, in front of the Czech Radio building, was no coincidence. It was an expression of the Czech public’s instinctive determination to defend Czech Radio as an independent source of information. That is why we consider this stretch of pavement in front of our building the most fitting place to commemorate those who lost their lives, while also reminding ourselves of our right to freedom and independence as an essential condition for fulfilling our mission.” After Zavoral, Czech President Petr Pavel took the stage to loud applause and chants of support. In his speech, he drew a parallel between the Soviet Union’s expansionist ambitions in the past and Russia’s aggressive policies today. “Although 58 years have now passed since the Warsaw Pact invasion of our country, the trauma of betrayal and the humiliation inflicted by our former allies remains deeply rooted in Czech society. As a result of this trauma, however, we as a nation could and should be more aware of and more sensitive to the aggressive and expansionist tendencies of today’s Russia, and perhaps also more resilient to its propaganda. Unfortunately, there are still many people who seek to understand and justify Vladimir Putin and the Russian regime for their actions.” President Pavel highlighted Ukraine’s courage in defending not only its own country but Europe as a whole. He ended his speech, much like the Czech Radio director, with an appeal to defend the freedom of public-service media in the Czech Republic. “Public-service media are once again facing pressure to restrict their freedom and independence, albeit in a more subtle way than the Russian-speaking soldiers with machine guns represented. Independent media are one of the fundamental pillars not only of our democracy, but of any democracy. Let us therefore allow ourselves to lose them as a result of their gradual dismantling.” Those assembled at the ceremony voiced their support for the public media loud and clear, and the speeches of the representatives of the ruling coalition, Finance Minister Alena Schillerová, and Chamber of Deputies Speaker Tomio Okamura, were almost drowned in whistling and booing. Photograph: Jonas Roosens/Belga Mag/AFP/Getty Images Florida Palestinian American activist arrested and ‘charged for trespassing at a public hearing’ Noura Erakat says a Florida mayor shortened speaking time and banned discussion of investment in Israeli bonds Alice Speri Wed 16 Sep 2026 15.17 EDT Last modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 12.12 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The human rights lawyer Noura Erakat was arrested on Tuesday at a Palm Beach county, Florida , budget hearing about the county’s more than $1bn investments in Israeli bonds. Erakat, a prominent Palestinian American activist, legal scholar and Guardian contributor, was one of several people in attendance at the public commission hearing who were forcibly removed by local law enforcement. The removal happened when the group attempted to speak out against the county’s investment in the bonds – the largest by a municipal government. Representatives for Palm Beach county did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Human rights group warns New York officials against investing public funds in Israeli bonds Read more In a video of Erakat’s arrest posted by Al Jazeera, two law enforcement officers are seen taking her away as she speaks about wanting to exercise “basic free speech”. Erakat said that she and other critics of the county’s investment in Israeli bonds had planned to make statements at the hearing but that when they arrived there, the county’s mayor, Sara Baxter, told those present they could only speak for one minute as opposed to the slotted three. She later said only residents would be allowed to speak and that people who applauded would be removed. Erakat also recalled that Baxter said that speakers could not address the Israeli bonds issue because they were a policy matter and not a budget one. When people spoke about the matter anyway, they were removed from the room. During a recess, police officers entered the room and “handpicked” people to remove, she added. “I insisted that I had a right to stay, they didn’t know what I was going to talk about, they were racially profiling me,” said Erakat. Investments in the Israeli bonds have become a controversial issue as US public opinion of Israel has plunged. In Florida, a group of residents sued Palm Beach county last year over the investment, which the group says was carried out in violation of local laws, including requirements that foreign investments meet certain ratings and prohibitions around investing for political reasons. The case was dismissed in August for lack of standing, but the plaintiffs are appealing the decision. “These millions of dollars should be going to local needs,” Lydia Ghuman, executive director of the Internationalist Law Center, which is representing the plaintiffs in that case, told the Guardian earlier this year. “The fact that they are being invested in bonds that are not beating the rate of inflation and propping up the economy of a foreign government is a sign of the special interests gripping local politics.” Nationwide, a coalition of groups has launched a “ Break the Bonds ” campaign encouraging advocacy for divestment at the local level, as well as targeting state and union pension funds and universities’ investments in Israel. Several candidates in recent primaries races have pledged to end public investments in Israeli bonds. “It’s becoming harder and harder to argue that these investments are being made purely for fiduciary or financially sound reasons,” said Michael Omer-Man, director of Israel-Palestine at the US-based human rights group Dawn. The group argued in a memo to elected officials earlier this year that investment of public funds in Israeli bonds violates both international law and fiduciary duties and may expose officials and beneficiaries alike to “substantial legal, ethical and financial risks”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Around 2-3 times a day Sign up to Breaking News US Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion Erakat said she was “rough-handled” and held, tightly cuffed, in the back of a police car for two hours before being shackled and transferred to a local jail, where she was released on bail. She was charged with a trespass misdemeanor. “It’s absolutely absurd that this is the reaction to a public hearing and that I would be charged for trespassing at a public hearing,” she said. “They were about to shut down the whole process and make it impossible to deal with the Israel bonds issue as a public matter. We talk about fascism but to see it play out so vividly was what compelled me to stay in the room honestly.” Charles Blaha, a former state department official and Dawn adviser who was also ejected from the room, said that the county commission had abruptly canceled the scheduled discussion. “The county knows the very problematic nature of the investment and the depth of public opposition, and is unable to defend the investment publicly,” he said. “Instead, the county suppressed legitimate free speech and public debate.” Explore more on these topics Florida Israel Freedom of speech US crime Middle East and north Africa news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness
